121378.m: The FOEN was created in 2006 from the SAEFL and the Federal Office for Water and Geology.

121567.q: Which feature do prokaryotes lack, unlike eukaryotes?
a: A nucleus with a nuclear envelope
121567.e: In prokaryotes, the DNA lies freely in the cytoplasm without being surrounded by a nuclear envelope. A cell membrane, ribosomes and cytoplasm, on the other hand, are found in all cells.

121568.q: Which two domains of life belong to the prokaryotes?
121568.e: In Carl Woese's three-domain system, bacteria and archaea are prokaryotic, and the eukaryotes form the third domain. Viruses are not considered living things with their own cells.
121568.m: Bacteria and archaea are the two groups of prokaryotes.

121569.q: What is the region in a bacterium's cytoplasm called where the ring-shaped chromosome lies?
121569.e: The nucleoid is a nuclear region without a membrane in which the bacterial chromosome is tightly packed. The nucleolus, by contrast, is part of the nucleus of eukaryotes.
121569.m: Bacterial DNA lies in the nucleoid without an envelope.

121570.q: Which type of ribosome do prokaryotes have?
121570.e: Prokaryotes have smaller 70S ribosomes, while eukaryotes have 80S ribosomes in the cytoplasm. Many antibiotics use this difference and specifically block the 70S ribosomes.

121571.q: What substance is the cell wall of most bacteria mainly made of?
121571.e: Murein, also called peptidoglycan, is a network of sugar chains and short peptides. Cellulose is found in plant cell walls, chitin in fungi and insects.
121571.m: The bacterial cell wall is made of murein.

121572.q: What are the long, rotating structures that many bacteria use to move called?
121572.e: Bacterial flagella are turned like a propeller by a motor in the cell envelope. Cilia and pseudopodia, by contrast, are found in eukaryotic cells.

121573.q: What are the small, usually ring-shaped DNA molecules called that bacteria can have in addition to their chromosome?
121573.e: Plasmids copy themselves independently of the chromosome and often carry useful extra genes. Plastids, by contrast, are organelles of plant cells.
121573.m: Plasmids are small rings of DNA in bacteria.

121574.q: After which Danish doctor is the staining method named that divides bacteria into two groups by the structure of their cell wall?
121574.e: Hans Christian Gram developed the stain in 1884. Bacteria with a thick cell wall layer stain blue-violet, those with a thin layer and an outer membrane stain red.
121574.m: Gram staining distinguishes bacteria by their cell wall.

121575.q: What is the reproductive cycle of a phage called in which the host cell bursts after new phages have formed?
121575.e: In the lytic cycle, the bacterium immediately produces new phages until the cell is dissolved and releases them. Lysis means dissolving.
121575.m: In the lytic cycle, the bacterial cell is destroyed.

121576.q: What is the phage DNA called that is built into the bacterial chromosome in the lysogenic cycle?
121576.e: The prophage is copied along with every cell division without killing the bacterium. Only under stress can it be cut out and trigger the production of new phages.
121576.m: A built-in phage is called a prophage.

121577.q: What is the protein shell called that surrounds the genetic material of a phage?
121577.e: The capsid consists of many identical protein building blocks. In typical phages such as T4, it sits as a head on a tail with fibres.
121577.m: The capsid protects a virus's genetic material.

121578.q: What did Alfred Hershey and Martha Chase prove with bacteriophages in 1952?
a: That DNA is the genetic material
That proteins are the genetic material
That viruses have their own cells
121578.e: They labelled the DNA with radioactive phosphorus and the proteins with radioactive sulphur. Only the labelled DNA got into the bacteria.
121578.m: The Hershey-Chase experiment proved that DNA carries genetic information.

121579.q: What would people like to use bacteriophages for more often in medicine?
121579.e: Phages attack particular bacteria specifically, including those against which antibiotics no longer work. This phage therapy has a long tradition, especially in Georgia.
121579.m: Phages are a hope against resistant bacteria.

121580.q: Why are bacteriophages basically harmless to humans?
a: They do not survive in water
They are bigger than human cells
They are digested by the stomach at once
121580.e: Phages use their tail fibres to recognise very specific surface structures of bacteria. They cannot dock onto human cells.

121581.q: What does the Greek part “phage” in “bacteriophage” mean?
121581.e: Phagein means to eat or devour in Greek. A bacteriophage is therefore literally a bacteria eater.

121582.q: What is the transfer of bacterial genes from one cell to another with the help of phages called?
121582.e: In transduction, phages accidentally package pieces of bacterial DNA and carry them into the next bacterium. In transformation, by contrast, a bacterium takes up free DNA from its surroundings.
121582.m: In transduction, phages carry bacterial genes.

121583.q: What is the transfer of plasmids between two bacteria through direct cell contact via a pilus called?
121583.e: In conjugation, a donor bacterium forms a bridge to the recipient and transfers a copy of the plasmid. In this way resistance genes spread quickly, even between different species.
121583.m: Conjugation transfers plasmids through direct contact.

121584.q: Which enzyme makes many bacteria resistant to penicillins by splitting the active substance?
121584.e: Beta-lactamases destroy the penicillin molecule before it can work. That is why penicillins are often combined with inhibitors such as clavulanic acid.

121585.q: What is the approach called that looks at antibiotic resistance in humans, animals and the environment together?
121585.e: Resistant bacteria move back and forth between people, farm animals, food and water. That is why, in the One Health approach, human and veterinary medicine, farming and environmental protection work together.
121585.m: Resistance is best fought with the One Health approach.

121586.q: Which evolutionary process explains why resistant bacteria increase during antibiotic treatment?
121586.e: The antibiotic kills sensitive bacteria, while resistant ones survive and multiply. In this way resistance spreads through the bacterial population.

121587.q: What is meant by horizontal gene transfer in bacteria?
a: Genes are exchanged between existing cells
Genes are only passed on to daughter cells
121587.e: In horizontal gene transfer, genes pass not through division but sideways from one bacterium to another. This can even happen between different bacterial species.
121587.m: Horizontal gene transfer spreads resistance genes between bacteria.

121588.q: When is a germ described as multi-resistant?
a: When it is resistant to several classes of antibiotics
When disinfectants do not affect it
121588.e: Multi-resistant germs no longer respond to several groups of antibiotics. This makes treatment difficult and expensive.
121588.m: Multi-resistant germs defy several groups of antibiotics.

121589.q: What is the main aim of the Swiss Strategy on Antibiotic Resistance (StAR)?
a: To keep antibiotics effective in the long term
To sell antibiotics without a prescription
121589.e: The StAR strategy was adopted by the Federal Council in 2015. It includes measures in human and veterinary medicine and in farming so that antibiotics remain effective.
121589.m: Switzerland fights antibiotic resistance with the StAR strategy.

121590.q: Which behaviour by patients encourages antibiotic resistance to develop?
a: Stopping or changing the course without talking to the doctor
Telling the doctor about side effects
121590.e: Anyone who stops antibiotics on their own, takes the wrong dose or later takes leftover tablets themselves exposes bacteria to the drug unnecessarily or insufficiently. This helps resistant germs survive.
121590.m: Take antibiotics exactly as the doctor prescribes.

121591.q: Which aminopenicillin is very often prescribed today, for example for middle ear infections?
121591.e: Amoxicillin is a penicillin with a wider range of action that is well absorbed from the gut. Ciprofloxacin, doxycycline and clarithromycin belong to other classes of antibiotics.
121591.m: Amoxicillin is a commonly used penicillin.

121592.q: What did Alexander Fleming observe in 1928 that led to the discovery of penicillin?
a: A mould stopped bacteria growing in a culture dish
121592.e: Fleming noticed that no bacteria grew around a mould of the genus Penicillium. The mould produced a substance that he called penicillin.

121593.q: Why was penicillin only used as a medicine more than ten years after its discovery?
a: It was difficult to make it pure and in large amounts
It was banned at the time
At first it only worked on plants
Nobody had recognised bacteria as germs
121593.e: Only around 1940 did Howard Florey and Ernst Chain in Oxford manage to purify penicillin and show its healing effect. For this they received the Nobel Prize with Fleming in 1945.
121593.m: Florey and Chain turned penicillin into a medicine.

121594.q: How does penicillin act on bacteria?
a: It blocks the building of the cell wall
It dissolves the cell membrane at once
121594.e: Penicillin blocks enzymes that cross-link the network of sugar chains and peptides in the cell wall. Growing bacteria therefore become unstable and burst.
121594.m: Penicillin disrupts the building of the bacterial cell wall.

121595.q: Which ring structure in the molecule is crucial for penicillin's effect?
121595.e: The strained four-membered beta-lactam ring binds to the enzymes that build the cell wall and blocks them. Cephalosporins also have this ring.
121595.m: Penicillins belong to the beta-lactam antibiotics.

121596.q: Against which bacteria does penicillin G mainly work?
121596.e: Gram-positive bacteria have a thick cell wall layer that is easy to reach. In gram-negative bacteria, an outer membrane protects the thin cell wall layer.
121596.m: Penicillin G works especially well against gram-positive germs.

121597.q: Why is penicillin G usually injected rather than swallowed?
a: It is destroyed by stomach acid
It does not dissolve in water
It is stored straight away by the liver
121597.e: Penicillin G is sensitive to acid and would be largely broken down in the stomach. Penicillin V is more stable in acid and can be taken as a tablet.

121598.q: Which unwanted reaction to penicillin is the best known?
121598.e: Penicillin allergies are among the most common drug allergies and range from skin rashes to anaphylactic shock. Discoloured teeth, by contrast, are typical of tetracyclines.

121599.q: What do staphylococci typically look like under the microscope?
a: Spheres in clusters like bunches of grapes
121599.e: Staphylé is the Greek word for a bunch of grapes. Spherical bacteria in chains, by contrast, are streptococci.
121599.m: Staphylococci lie together like bunches of grapes.

121600.q: Where does Staphylococcus aureus live in many healthy people without making them ill?
121600.e: Around 20 to 30 per cent of people carry Staphylococcus aureus in their nose, some of them permanently. It only becomes dangerous when it gets into the body, for example through wounds.
121600.m: Many healthy people carry staphylococci in their nose.

121601.q: Which measure is most important in hospital to prevent MRSA from being passed on?
a: Taking the temperature of all visitors
121601.e: MRSA is mainly carried from patient to patient on the hands of staff. Hand disinfection breaks this route most effectively.
121601.m: Hand disinfection stops MRSA from spreading.

121602.q: What does the “R” in the abbreviation MRSA stand for?
121602.e: MRSA means methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus. These bacteria are not affected by methicillin and related antibiotics such as penicillins.
121602.m: MRSA is resistant to methicillin and related antibiotics.

121603.q: Why are MRSA infections harder to treat than ordinary staphylococcal infections?
a: Many common antibiotics no longer work
121603.e: The usual beta-lactam antibiotics fail against MRSA. Doctors have to switch to a few reserve drugs such as vancomycin, which can have more side effects.
121603.m: Many common antibiotics do not work against MRSA.

121604.q: What does decolonisation mean for MRSA carriers?
a: The bacteria are removed from the skin and mucous membranes
The person is moved to another country
The bacteria are grown in the laboratory
The person is given a vaccine against MRSA
121604.e: Nasal ointments and antiseptic washes, for example, are used for several days. The aim is that the person no longer carries the bacteria and passes them on.

121605.q: In which decade was MRSA first described, shortly after methicillin was introduced?
121605.e: Methicillin came onto the market in 1959, and resistant strains were already described in Great Britain in 1961. This shows how quickly bacteria adapt.
121605.m: MRSA appeared as early as the 1960s.

121606.e: Prions contain no genetic material but are proteins with an abnormal three-dimensional folding. This makes them fundamentally different from viruses and bacteria.
121606.m: Prions are disease-causing proteins without genetic material.

121607.q: Who coined the term prion and received the Nobel Prize in Medicine for it in 1997?
121607.e: In 1982 the American Stanley Prusiner described prions as protein-like infectious particles. His theory was controversial for a long time.

121608.q: Which animal disease, which also concerned Switzerland in the 1990s, is caused by prions?
121608.e: Bovine spongiform encephalopathy, known as mad cow disease, also occurred in Swiss cattle. The other diseases are caused by viruses.
121608.m: BSE is a prion disease of cattle.

121609.q: Which human disease is caused by prions?
121609.e: Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease quickly destroys nerve tissue in the brain and is fatal. One variant has been linked to eating beef contaminated with BSE.
121609.m: Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease is a prion disease.

121610.q: How do prions multiply in the body?
a: They make normal proteins fold wrongly too
They build their genetic material into the DNA
They form spores in the nerve cells
121610.e: A misfolded prion protein acts like a template and changes the shape of healthy proteins. This creates a chain reaction, and the faulty proteins build up as deposits.
121610.m: Prions multiply by refolding healthy proteins.

121611.q: Why do surgical instruments need special treatment if prions are suspected?
a: Prions survive many usual sterilisation methods
121611.e: Prions are very resistant to heat, radiation and many disinfectants. That is why especially strict cleaning rules apply to them.

121612.q: What is the prion disease of sheep and goats called?
121612.e: Scrapie has been known since the 18th century; sick animals often rub themselves against fences. Distemper, foot rot and mange have other causes.
121612.m: Scrapie is the prion disease of sheep.

121613.q: In which country did the prion disease kuru occur?
121613.e: Kuru affected the Fore people in the highlands of Papua New Guinea. It was passed on through ritual funeral customs and disappeared after these were given up.
121613.m: Kuru was a prion disease in Papua New Guinea.

121614.q: Which enzyme in retroviruses copies RNA into DNA?
121614.e: Reverse transcriptase reverses the usual flow of information from DNA to RNA. This is also where the name retrovirus comes from.
121614.m: Retroviruses copy their RNA into DNA.

121615.q: Which is the best-known retrovirus that makes humans ill?
121615.e: The human immunodeficiency virus is a retrovirus and, if untreated, can lead to the disease AIDS. Flu, measles and hepatitis A viruses are not retroviruses.
121615.m: HIV is one of the retroviruses.

121616.q: Which immune cells does HIV mainly attack?
121616.e: HIV docks onto the surface protein CD4, which is carried mainly by T helper cells. If these cells fail, the whole immune defence is weakened.
121616.m: HIV mainly destroys T helper cells.

121617.q: What is the DNA of a retrovirus called once it is built into the host cell's genome?
121617.e: The provirus stays permanently in the cell's genome and is copied with every division. That is why an HIV infection cannot yet be cured completely.
121617.m: Built-in retrovirus DNA is called a provirus.

121618.q: Which enzyme of a retrovirus builds the newly made viral DNA into the host genome?
121618.e: Integrase cuts open the host DNA and inserts the viral DNA. Integrase inhibitors are an important part of HIV treatment today.
121618.m: Integrase builds viral DNA into the genome.

121619.q: Why was the discovery of reverse transcriptase around 1970 so important?
a: It showed that genetic information can also flow from RNA to DNA
It showed that viruses have no genetic information
It proved that DNA is made of proteins
It led directly to a cure for AIDS
121619.e: People had assumed that information only flows from DNA to RNA. But retroviruses copy their RNA into DNA. The discoverers received the Nobel Prize in 1975.
121619.m: Retroviruses reverse the flow of information.

121620.q: What kind of genetic material do retroviruses carry in the virus particle?
121620.e: Each retrovirus particle contains two copies of single-stranded RNA. Only in the host cell is it turned into double-stranded DNA.
121620.m: Retroviruses carry their genetic material as RNA.

121621.q: What are endogenous retroviruses in the human genome?
a: Remains of old virus infections passed down for generations
Active viruses that make every person ill
Bacteria living in the cell nucleus
Genes that only appear during illness
121621.e: Millions of years ago, retroviruses built their DNA into the germ cells of our ancestors. These traces have been inherited ever since and are mostly inactive.
121621.m: Our genome contains many remains of old retroviruses.

121622.q: What is typical of a parasite?
a: It lives at the expense of a host
It lives only on dead material
121622.e: A parasite takes nutrients from its host and harms it, but usually does not kill it straight away. When both partners benefit, it is called symbiosis.
121622.m: A parasite lives at the expense of its host.

121623.q: Which of these organisms is an ectoparasite?
121623.e: Ectoparasites live on the outside of the host's body, like the tick on the skin. Tapeworm, roundworm and liver fluke live inside the body and are endoparasites.
121623.m: Ectoparasites live on the outside of their host.

121624.q: What is the host called in which a parasite reaches its adult stage?
121624.e: In the definitive host, the parasite becomes adult and reproduces. Only larval or young stages live in the intermediate host.
121624.m: A parasite becomes adult in the definitive host.

121625.q: Which animals are the typical intermediate hosts of the fox tapeworm?
121625.e: Mice take in the worm eggs, and larvae grow in their liver. When a fox eats the mouse, the cycle is complete; humans can be infected as accidental hosts.
121625.m: Mice are the intermediate hosts of the fox tapeworm.

121626.q: What is a relationship called in which one partner benefits and the other neither benefits nor is harmed?
121626.e: In commensalism, an animal might for example use another's food scraps without harming it. In parasitism, by contrast, the host is harmed.
121626.m: Commensals help themselves without harming their partner.

121627.q: Which native bird is a well-known brood parasite?
121627.e: The female cuckoo lays her eggs in other birds' nests. The host birds raise the cuckoo chick, often at the expense of their own young.
121627.m: The cuckoo has its young raised by other birds.

121628.q: Which bacterial disease is most often passed on by ticks in Switzerland?
121628.e: Lyme disease is caused by bacteria of the genus Borrelia and can be treated with antibiotics. There is a vaccine against TBE, which is also passed on by ticks but is caused by a virus.
121628.m: In Switzerland, ticks mainly pass on Lyme disease.

121629.q: Which animal is the definitive host of the parasite Toxoplasma gondii?
121629.e: Only in cats and other felines can Toxoplasma complete its full life cycle. Mice and also humans are intermediate hosts.
121629.m: Cats are the definitive hosts of Toxoplasma.

121630.q: Which mosquitoes pass the malaria parasites on to humans?
121630.e: Only females of the genus Anopheles pass on plasmodia when they suck blood. The tiger mosquito passes on other diseases, such as dengue.
121630.m: Malaria is spread by Anopheles mosquitoes.

121631.q: To which group of disease-causing organisms do plasmodia belong?
121631.e: Plasmodia are single-celled organisms with a nucleus, in other words eukaryotes. That is why antibiotics against bacteria do not help against malaria.
121631.m: Malaria is caused by single-celled organisms.

121632.q: Which species of Plasmodium causes the most dangerous form of malaria?
121632.e: Plasmodium falciparum causes falciparum malaria, which is often fatal if untreated. Infected blood cells stick together in small vessels, for example in the brain.
121632.m: Plasmodium falciparum is the most dangerous malaria parasite.

121633.q: Which blood cells do plasmodia attack in the human body?
121633.e: The parasites multiply in the red blood cells and make them burst. Many cells bursting at the same time leads to bouts of fever.
121633.m: Plasmodia multiply in red blood cells.

121634.q: Which organ do plasmodia travel to first after a mosquito bite?
121634.e: The parasites first multiply unnoticed in liver cells. Only after that do they get into the blood and cause the signs of illness.
121634.m: Plasmodia first multiply in the liver.

121635.q: For discovering which malaria drug did the Chinese researcher Tu Youyou receive the Nobel Prize in 2015?
121635.e: Tu Youyou obtained artemisinin from sweet wormwood, a plant used in traditional Chinese medicine. Combination therapies with artemisinin are standard today against falciparum malaria.
121635.m: Artemisinin is an important malaria drug from a plant.

121636.q: Which inherited blood disease, in its mild form with only one copy of the gene, partly protects against malaria?
121636.e: Carriers with one copy of the sickle cell gene are less likely to become seriously ill with falciparum malaria. That is why the gene is common in the malaria regions of Africa.
121636.m: The sickle cell gene gives some protection against malaria.

121637.q: What best protects travellers in malaria regions from infection?
a: Protection against mosquitoes and, depending on the region, preventive medicines
Having no contact with sick people
A single vaccination before the trip
121637.e: Malaria is spread by mosquito bites, not by water or direct contact. Mosquito nets, long clothing and insect repellent help, and in some regions tablets as well.
121637.m: Protection against mosquitoes is the main defence against malaria.

a: An infection caught in hospital or a care home
An infection that only affects animals
121638.e: Nosocomial comes from the Greek nosokomeion, hospital. It means infections that arise in connection with a stay or treatment in a healthcare facility.

121639.q: From when after admission to hospital is an infection usually considered nosocomial?
a: At the earliest about 48 hours after admission
121639.e: If an infection only appears after about 48 hours and was not present or incubating on admission, it is put down to the hospital. Earlier infections were usually brought in from home.
121639.m: After about 48 hours in hospital, a new infection counts as nosocomial.

121640.q: Which doctor reduced childbed fever in Vienna in 1847 through handwashing with chlorinated lime?
121640.e: Semmelweis realised that doctors were carrying disease material from corpses to patients. With a chlorinated lime solution, the death rate on his ward fell sharply.
121640.m: Ignaz Semmelweis is considered a pioneer of hand hygiene.

121641.q: Which medical device especially increases the risk of a urinary tract infection in hospital?
121641.e: Bacteria can get directly into the bladder through the catheter tube. That is why a urinary catheter should only stay in for as long as necessary.
121641.m: Urinary catheters encourage urinary tract infections.

121642.q: What is the Swiss national centre for infection prevention called, which records hospital infections?
121642.e: Swissnoso carries out surveillance of wound infections after operations and runs infection prevention programmes. Swissmedic, by contrast, is the authority for medicines.
121642.m: Swissnoso deals with hospital infections in Switzerland.

121643.q: According to the WHO, for how long should hands be rubbed with an alcohol-based disinfectant?
121643.e: The WHO recommends rubbing in the product for 20 to 30 seconds until the hands are dry. In this way every part of the hands is reached.
121643.m: Hand disinfection takes about half a minute.

121644.q: How many moments for hand hygiene does the WHO describe for healthcare staff?
121644.e: The moments are: before touching a patient, before clean or aseptic procedures, after contact with body fluids, after touching a patient and after touching the patient's surroundings.
121644.m: The WHO names five moments for hand hygiene.

121645.q: What is the federal strategy for monitoring, preventing and fighting hospital infections called?
121645.e: The Federal Council adopted the NOSO strategy in 2016. It aims to reduce infections in hospitals and care homes in Switzerland.
121645.m: The NOSO strategy fights hospital infections in Switzerland.

121646.q: Why are patients in intensive care especially at risk of hospital infections?
a: They often have catheters, tubes and a weakened immune system
They always lie in single rooms
121646.e: Breathing tubes and venous catheters open direct routes into the body for germs. In addition, the defences of seriously ill people are often weakened.
121646.m: Intensive care patients have a high risk of infection.

121647.q: According to today's definition, what is sepsis?
a: Life-threatening organ dysfunction caused by a misdirected response to an infection
Harmless reddening of the skin after an insect bite
121647.e: Since the Sepsis-3 definition of 2016, the focus is not on the infection itself but on the excessive and harmful reaction of the body. It can make organs such as the kidneys, lungs or circulation fail.
121647.m: In sepsis, the defence reaction damages the body's own organs.

121648.q: Which everyday expression is often used for sepsis?
121648.e: The term blood poisoning is widespread but inaccurate, as there is no poison in the strict sense. Lockjaw is an everyday name for tetanus.
121648.m: In everyday language, sepsis is called blood poisoning.

121649.q: Which signs during an infection can point to the start of sepsis?
121649.e: If a sick person breathes noticeably fast, seems confused or has low blood pressure, sepsis may be present. Then medical help is needed immediately.
121649.m: Fast breathing and confusion during an infection are warning signs.

121650.q: What is typical of septic shock?
a: A drop in blood pressure that needs circulation-supporting drugs despite fluids
High fever with no other symptoms
121650.e: In septic shock, the circulation is so badly disturbed that vasopressors are needed despite drips. The death rate is then especially high.
121650.m: Septic shock is the most severe form of sepsis.

121651.q: According to guidelines, within what time should antibiotics be given if septic shock is suspected?
a: Only after all lab results are in
121651.e: With every hour of delay, the risk of death rises considerably. That is why international guidelines recommend giving antibiotics within the first hour if possible.

121652.q: According to a large study in “The Lancet”, roughly how many deaths worldwide in 2017 were due to sepsis?
121652.e: The study estimated around 49 million cases of sepsis and about 11 million deaths for 2017. That was around one fifth of all deaths worldwide.
121652.m: Sepsis is one of the most common causes of death worldwide.

121653.q: Which people have an especially high risk of developing sepsis?
a: Babies, older people and people with weak immune systems
121653.e: In very young, old or immunocompromised people, the defence system is less able to contain an infection. Sepsis is therefore more common in them.
121653.m: Very young, old and immunocompromised people are especially at risk.

121654.q: Which blood value is measured in sepsis as a sign that the tissues are not getting enough oxygen?
121654.e: When cells lack oxygen, they get energy anaerobically and produce lactate. A raised lactate level shows a dangerous circulatory disorder.
121654.m: A high lactate level warns of a lack of oxygen in the tissues.

121655.q: If sepsis is suspected, what should be taken if possible before the first dose of antibiotics?
a: A saliva sample for a genetic test
121655.e: In blood cultures, the germs can be grown and tested for resistance. After antibiotics have been given, they often no longer grow, so the blood is taken beforehand.
121655.m: Blood cultures help to find the germ causing sepsis.

121656.q: In which year did the WHO declare the spread of COVID-19 a pandemic?
121656.e: On 11 March 2020, the WHO classified the worldwide spread of the coronavirus SARS-CoV-2 as a pandemic. The first cases had appeared in China at the end of 2019.
121656.m: The WHO declared COVID-19 a pandemic in March 2020.

121657.q: On which day did the WHO constitution come into force in 1948, a day now marked as World Health Day?
121657.e: The WHO constitution came into force on 7 April 1948. Since then, World Health Day has been held every year on this day with a focus theme.
121657.m: World Health Day is on 7 April.

121658.q: Which list has the WHO published regularly since 1977 as a guide for healthcare?
a: The Model List of Essential Medicines
The list of World Heritage Sites
The Red List of Threatened Species
The list of banned doping substances
121658.e: The model list names medicines that are important for basic healthcare in every country. It is revised about every two years.
121658.m: The WHO keeps a list of essential medicines.

121659.q: Who is Director-General of the WHO (as of 2026)?
121659.e: The Ethiopian Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus has led the WHO since 2017 and was re-elected in 2022. Margaret Chan was his predecessor, and António Guterres is UN Secretary-General.
121659.m: Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus leads the WHO.

121660.q: What is the highest decision-making body of the WHO, in which all member states are represented, called?
121660.e: The World Health Assembly meets every year in Geneva and sets the WHO's policy and budget. The Security Council is a body of the UN.
121660.m: The World Health Assembly is the highest body of the WHO.

121661.q: What status does the WHO have in the United Nations system?
a: It is a specialised agency of the UN
It is an authority of the European Union
121661.e: The WHO is a legally independent specialised agency of the United Nations with its own member states. It coordinates international health work.
121661.m: The WHO belongs to the UN as a specialised agency.

121662.q: Why does the WHO call for antibiotics to be used only in a targeted and sparing way?
a: So that fewer resistant bacteria develop
Because antibiotics only work in winter
Because there are hardly any antibiotics left worldwide
121662.e: Every use of antibiotics favours bacteria that are not affected by them. If resistance becomes more common, the medicines no longer work for dangerous infections.
121662.m: Using antibiotics sparingly slows down resistance.

121663.q: How does the WHO constitution define health?
a: As a state of complete physical, mental and social well-being
As simply the absence of illness
As the ability to work fully
As the result of regular visits to the doctor
121663.e: The definition in the constitution stresses that health is more than the absence of disease or infirmity. It includes mental and social well-being.
121663.m: For the WHO, health is more than the absence of illness.

121963.q: Which antibody class drives the classic immediate-type allergy?
121963.e: Allergen-specific immunoglobulin E sits on mast cells and, at renewed contact with the allergen, triggers the release of messenger substances.
121963.m: IgE plays the main role in immediate-type allergy.

121964.q: Against which invaders is immunoglobulin E originally mainly directed?
121964.e: Together with mast cells and eosinophil granulocytes, IgE helps to fight worms and other parasites. In allergies, this defence is directed against harmless substances.
121964.m: Originally, IgE serves to fight parasites.

121965.q: Which antibody was discovered in the 1960s and explained how allergic reactions are triggered?
121965.e: The married couple Ishizaka in the USA and Johansson and Bennich in Sweden described IgE in 1966 and 1967. This identified the antibody that drives immediate-type allergies.
121965.m: IgE was discovered in the 1960s as the allergy antibody.

121966.q: Why is IgE found only in very small amounts in the blood, even though it is so important in allergies?
a: Most of it is attached firmly to mast cells
It is excreted through the kidneys at once
It is only found in the gut
It breaks down when blood is taken
121966.e: IgE is the rarest antibody class in serum. Most of it is bound to mast cells and basophil granulocytes and waits there for the allergen.
121966.m: IgE is the rarest antibody class in the blood.

121967.q: Which messenger substance is released from mast cells during an allergic reaction and causes itching and swelling?
121967.e: When an allergen binds to IgE on mast cells, they release histamine. Antihistamines block its effect.
121967.m: Histamine from mast cells causes allergic symptoms.

121968.q: What is an allergy treatment called in which you receive increasing amounts of the allergen over years?
121968.e: In desensitisation, also called specific immunotherapy, the immune system slowly gets used to the allergen. The IgE-driven reaction becomes weaker as a result.
121968.m: Desensitisation gets the immune system used to an allergen.

121969.q: Which cells make IgE and other antibodies?
121969.e: Activated B cells mature into plasma cells and produce antibodies. Messenger substances from T helper cells, such as interleukin-4, get them to make IgE.
121969.m: Plasma cells produce antibodies, including IgE.

121970.q: Which medicine is injected first in a severe allergic shock?
121970.e: In anaphylaxis, triggered by IgE and mast cells, adrenaline narrows the blood vessels and widens the airways. People with allergies often carry an emergency auto-injector for this.
121970.m: In an allergic shock, adrenaline helps first.

121971.q: Which messenger substance is stored in the granules of mast cells and causes itching and swelling?
121971.e: Histamine widens blood vessels, makes them leakier and irritates nerve endings. This leads to redness, weals and itching.
121971.m: Mast cells store large amounts of histamine.

121972.q: In which kind of reaction do mast cells play a central role?
121972.e: Mast cells carry antibodies of the IgE type on their surface. When an allergen such as pollen binds to them, they release histamine within minutes.
121972.m: Mast cells trigger immediate allergic reactions.

121973.q: Where does the name “mast cell” come from?
a: They were thought to be well-fed cells
They are found mainly in the gut
They were first found in animals being fattened
They are shaped like a ship's mast
121973.e: Their discoverer believed that the cells, packed with granules, were “fattened” (German “gemästet”) and served to nourish the tissue. The name stayed, even though the idea was wrong.
121973.m: The mast cell's name comes from its fattened appearance.

121974.q: What is it called when an activated mast cell releases its stored granules?
121974.e: In degranulation, the storage granules merge with the cell membrane and release histamine and other mediators. This happens within seconds to minutes.
121974.m: An activated mast cell empties its granules by degranulation.

121975.q: Where do the precursors of mast cells develop?
121975.e: Mast cells come from blood-forming stem cells in the bone marrow. Their precursors move into the tissue and only mature there.
121975.m: The precursors of mast cells come from the bone marrow.

121976.q: What is a disease called in which mast cells multiply abnormally and build up in the tissue?
121976.e: In mastocytosis, mast cells build up in the skin, bone marrow or other organs. Those affected have a higher risk of severe allergic reactions.
121976.m: In mastocytosis there are too many mast cells.

121977.q: Which medicines block the effect of histamine from mast cells, for example in hay fever?
121977.e: Antihistamines occupy the histamine receptors so that the released histamine has less effect. Sneezing, itching and watery eyes ease off.
121977.m: Antihistamines damp down the effect of histamine.

121978.q: Which life-threatening reaction can occur when very many mast cells throughout the body release histamine at the same time?
121978.e: In anaphylaxis, the blood vessels throughout the body widen, blood pressure falls and the airways can swell shut. It is treated immediately with adrenaline.
121978.m: A massive release of histamine can trigger anaphylactic shock.

121979.q: What is hyposensitisation also called in technical language?
121979.e: In specific immunotherapy, the body receives the allergen that causes the problem in increasing doses. The aim is for the immune system to tolerate the substance again.

121980.q: How long does hyposensitisation usually last?
121980.e: So that the immune system changes for the long term, specialist societies recommend treatment for about three to five years. Shorter treatments work for less long.
121980.m: Hyposensitisation needs several years of patience.

121981.q: How is the allergen given in sublingual immunotherapy?
121981.e: Sublingual means “under the tongue”. Drops or tablets with the allergen are absorbed there instead of being injected.
121981.m: In sublingual therapy, the allergen goes under the tongue.

121982.q: For which allergy is hyposensitisation carried out especially often?
121982.e: Hay fever caused by grass or tree pollen is one of the most common allergies. Hyposensitisation can clearly ease the symptoms for years.
121982.m: Hay fever is often treated with hyposensitisation.

121983.q: Which messenger substance causes itching, sneezing and swelling in an allergic reaction?
121983.e: On contact with the allergen, mast cells release histamine. It widens vessels and irritates nerves, which causes the typical symptoms.
121983.m: Histamine causes the typical allergy symptoms.

121984.q: Why do patients usually have to stay at the surgery for about 30 minutes after a hyposensitisation injection?
a: Because of the risk of anaphylaxis
Because the allergen first has to take effect
So that the doctor can lower the blood pressure
Because the injection is removed again
121984.e: The injection contains the allergen and can rarely trigger a severe allergic reaction. Such reactions usually happen early and can then be treated immediately.
121984.m: After the injection, you wait at the surgery because of possible anaphylaxis.

121985.q: For which allergy is hyposensitisation especially effective and can even save lives?
121985.e: In insect venom allergies, the treatment protects most of those treated from severe reactions if they are stung again. It is not suitable for the other complaints named.
121985.m: Hyposensitisation works especially well against insect venom allergy.

121986.q: What is the first phase of hyposensitisation called, in which the dose of allergen is gradually increased?
121986.e: First the dose is increased up to the maximum dose. Then comes the maintenance phase with a constant dose at longer intervals.
121986.m: Hyposensitisation starts with the build-up phase.

a: An inherited tendency to make IgE against substances in the environment
An allergy that only occurs in adults
An inflammation of the joints caused by autoantibodies
An inborn inability to make antibodies
121987.e: People with atopy make IgE more easily against harmless substances such as pollen or house dust mites. This can lead to hay fever, asthma or eczema.
121987.m: Atopy is an inherited readiness for IgE-driven allergies.

121988.q: Which condition usually comes first in the so-called “atopic march”?
121988.e: The atopic march often begins in infancy with atopic eczema. Later, food allergies, hay fever and asthma can follow.
121988.m: The atopic march usually starts with atopic eczema.

121989.q: What does the Greek word “atopia”, from which the term atopy comes, mean?
a: Being out of place or unusual
121989.e: Atopia literally means “without a place” and referred to something unusual. In 1923 Coca and Cooke chose the word for the strange oversensitivity to harmless substances.

121990.q: What does the hygiene hypothesis say about how allergies develop?
a: Little contact with microbes in childhood increases the risk of allergy
Allergies are passed on by bacteria
121990.e: The hypothesis assumes that the immune system must get to know many microbes early on. If this contact is missing, it is later more likely to react to harmless substances.
121990.m: Early contact with microbes probably protects against allergies.

121991.q: According to studies from Switzerland, Austria and Germany, which children have allergies less often?
a: Children from traditional farms with livestock
Children from flats in big cities
Children who have never had pets
121991.e: Studies such as the ALEX study showed that early contact with cowsheds and raw milk lowers the risk of allergy. This is explained by the variety of microbes in the surroundings.
121991.m: Farm children get allergies less often.

121992.q: Against which substances do people with atopy typically develop allergies?
121992.e: In atopy, the immune system reacts with IgE to substances in the environment that are actually harmless, such as pollen, animal hair or house dust mites.
121992.m: People with atopy react to harmless substances in the environment.

121993.q: Which skin test is often used to check which allergens someone reacts to?
121993.e: In the skin prick test, drops containing allergens are put on the forearm and the skin is pricked lightly. If a weal forms, the person is sensitised.
121993.m: The skin prick test shows allergies on the skin.

121994.q: Which term describes the rise in allergies in industrialised countries since the middle of the 20th century?
121994.e: In many industrialised countries, the share of people with hay fever and asthma has risen sharply. Experts therefore speak of an allergy epidemic.
121994.m: Allergies have risen sharply in industrialised countries.

121995.q: Which feature typically distinguishes bronchial asthma from COPD?
a: The narrowing of the airways is largely reversible
Asthma only affects the air sacs
Asthma is always caused by smoking
There is no inflammation at all in asthma
121995.e: In asthma, the narrowing of the bronchi improves clearly on its own or with medicines. In COPD it largely remains.
121995.m: In asthma, the narrowing of the airways is reversible.

121996.q: Which spirometry value shows how much air you can breathe out forcefully in the first second?
121996.e: FEV1 stands for forced expiratory volume in one second. During an asthma attack this value drops considerably.

121997.q: Which simple device can people with asthma use to monitor their breathing at home?
121997.e: The peak flow meter measures the highest speed at which you can breathe out. Falling values give early warning of things getting worse.
121997.m: A peak flow meter is used to check asthma at home.

121998.q: Which substance is a typical short-acting reliever inhaler that quickly widens the bronchi during an asthma attack?
121998.e: Salbutamol is a beta-2 agonist and relaxes the muscles of the bronchi within a few minutes. It eases the attack but does not treat the inflammation.
121998.m: Salbutamol quickly widens the bronchi when you are short of breath.

121999.q: Which group of medicines treats the inflammation of the airways in asthma in the long term?
121999.e: Inhaled corticosteroids damp down the chronic inflammation directly in the bronchi. They are taken regularly, even when there are no symptoms.
121999.m: Inhaled steroids fight the inflammation in asthma.

122000.q: What is a severe asthma attack called that does not ease despite the usual emergency medicines?
122000.e: In status asthmaticus, the severe breathlessness continues and can become life-threatening. It must be treated in hospital.
122000.m: A severe asthma attack that does not end is called status asthmaticus.

122001.q: Which whistling breathing sound when breathing out is typical of an asthma attack?
122001.e: Wheezing happens when air is forced through narrowed small bronchi. It is heard mainly when breathing out.
122001.m: Whistling wheezing when breathing out is typical of asthma.

122002.q: Why should you rinse your mouth after inhaling a steroid spray for asthma?
a: To prevent a fungal infection in the mouth
So that the spray works more strongly
To prevent tooth decay from sugar
So that the bronchi widen faster
122002.e: Some of the steroid stays in the mouth and throat and weakens the local defence there. Rinsing prevents fungal infections and hoarseness.
122002.m: Rinse your mouth after using a steroid spray.

122003.q: Which white blood cells are typically found in greater numbers in the phlegm in allergic asthma?
122003.e: In allergic asthma, eosinophil granulocytes move into the wall of the bronchi and keep the inflammation going. Their number is raised in the sputum and often in the blood too.
122003.m: In allergic asthma, eosinophils are increased.

122004.q: Which antibody class triggers immediate-type allergy?
122004.e: In immediate-type allergy, IgE antibodies sit on mast cells. When the allergen meets them, the mast cells release histamine.
122004.m: Immediate-type allergies are triggered by IgE.

122005.q: How quickly does an immediate-type allergy typically start after contact with the allergen?
a: After about one to two days
122005.e: Because the IgE is already waiting on the mast cells, histamine is released almost at once. That is why this form is called the immediate type.

122006.q: What is the most severe form of immediate-type allergy, affecting the whole body, called?
122006.e: In anaphylactic shock, blood pressure and circulation drop, and the airways can swell shut. Without quick treatment it can be fatal.
122006.m: Anaphylactic shock is the most severe immediate-type reaction.

122007.q: Which medicine is the most important emergency treatment for anaphylactic shock?
122007.e: Adrenaline narrows the blood vessels, stabilises the circulation and widens the bronchi. People at risk therefore often carry an adrenaline auto-injector.

122008.q: Which skin test is most often used to check for an immediate-type allergy?
122008.e: In the skin prick test, a drop of allergen solution is put on the skin and the skin is pricked lightly. A weal after about 15 to 20 minutes points to sensitisation.
122008.m: The skin prick test shows immediate-type allergies on the skin.

122009.q: Why can someone with a birch pollen allergy get a tingling in the mouth when eating a raw apple?
a: Because of a cross-allergy caused by similar proteins
Because apples produce a lot of histamine
Because of poisoning from fruit acid
122009.e: The main birch allergen resembles a protein in apples, so the IgE recognises both. Cooking usually destroys this apple protein.
122009.m: Birch pollen allergy and apple allergy are often cross-allergies.

122010.q: What is the inflammation called that can appear again a few hours after the first immediate-type reaction?
122010.e: Besides histamine, mast cells also make substances that attract inflammatory cells. These cause a second wave of symptoms hours later.
122010.m: A late-phase reaction can follow the immediate reaction.

122011.q: Why does an allergy usually only show itself at repeated contact with the allergen?
a: At the first contact, the body first has to make the matching antibodies
At the first contact, the allergen is still too small
The body does not notice the first contact at all
Allergens are excreted at once the first time
122011.e: At the first contact, the immune system is sensitised and makes IgE. Only at a later contact does the allergic reaction happen.

122012.q: What does the word “allergy” literally mean in Greek?
122012.e: Allergy comes from the Greek allos for “other” and ergon for “activity”. It means a changed reaction of the body to substances that are actually harmless.
122012.m: Allergy literally means a different reaction.

122013.q: Which joints are typically affected first, and on both sides, in rheumatoid arthritis?
a: The knuckles and middle finger joints
The joints of the lower spine
122013.e: The inflammation usually begins symmetrically in the small joints of the hands. The joints nearest the fingertips, by contrast, are typically spared.
122013.m: Rheumatoid arthritis first affects the knuckles and middle finger joints.

122014.q: Which pattern of complaints in the morning is typical of rheumatoid arthritis?
a: Long-lasting morning stiffness of the joints
122014.e: The inflamed joints are often stiff for more than half an hour in the morning. In osteoarthritis, stiffness when getting going usually lasts only a few minutes.
122014.m: Long morning stiffness points to rheumatoid arthritis.

122015.q: To which kind of disease does rheumatoid arthritis belong?
a: Inherited diseases caused by a single gene
122015.e: In rheumatoid arthritis, the immune system wrongly attacks the body's own tissue in the joints. This leads to lasting inflammation.
122015.m: In rheumatoid arthritis, the immune system attacks the body's own joints.

122016.q: What fundamentally distinguishes rheumatoid arthritis from osteoarthritis?
a: It is an inflammation, not wear and tear
It is caused by an accident
It only affects the bones, never the joints
122016.e: Osteoarthritis develops through wear of the cartilage. Rheumatoid arthritis, on the other hand, is an inflammatory disease of the immune system.
122016.m: Arthritis means inflammation, osteoarthritis means wear and tear.

122017.q: Why should rheumatoid arthritis be treated as early as possible?
a: So that the joints are not permanently destroyed
Because otherwise it turns into osteoarthritis
Because medicines are banned later on
122017.e: The inflammation gradually attacks cartilage and bone. Early treatment slows this process and keeps the joints moving.
122017.m: If treated early, the joints stay healthy for longer.

122018.q: What do most medicines against rheumatoid arthritis do?
a: They damp down the overactive immune system
They kill bacteria in the joint
122018.e: Because the immune system attacks the joints, the medicines slow down the defence in a targeted way. As a result, inflammation, pain and swelling ease.
122018.m: Medicines for rheumatism slow down the immune system.

122019.q: Which tissue layer in the joint is inflamed first in rheumatoid arthritis?
a: The inner lining of the joint
The outer lining of the bone
The tendon sheath of the calf
122019.e: The inflamed inner lining of the joint (synovium) grows excessively and forms what is known as pannus. This gradually destroys cartilage and bone.
122019.m: Rheumatoid arthritis starts in the inner lining of the joint.

122020.q: Who gets rheumatoid arthritis more often?
122020.e: Women are affected about two to three times more often than men. The disease usually starts in middle adulthood.
122020.m: More women than men get rheumatoid arthritis.

122021.q: What are the firm lumps under the skin called that appear in some people with rheumatoid arthritis on outer surfaces such as the elbow?
122021.e: Rheumatoid nodules are inflamed lumps of tissue at places under pressure. Heberden's nodes, by contrast, belong to osteoarthritis of the joints nearest the fingertips.
122021.m: Rheumatoid nodules often sit on the elbows.

122022.q: Which skin sign on the face is typical of systemic lupus erythematosus?
122022.e: The redness stretches across the cheeks and the bridge of the nose and looks like a butterfly. It often gets worse after exposure to the sun.
122022.m: A butterfly rash on the face is typical of lupus.

122023.q: What are many autoantibodies directed against in systemic lupus erythematosus?
a: Parts of the cell nucleus such as DNA
122023.e: In lupus, the immune system makes antibodies against parts of the body's own cell nuclei. Antibodies against double-stranded DNA are especially typical.
122023.m: In lupus, antibodies attack parts of the body's own cell nuclei.

122024.q: Which screening test for autoantibodies against cell nuclei is almost always positive in lupus?
122024.e: Antinuclear antibodies (ANA) are found in almost all patients with systemic lupus. A negative test therefore makes the diagnosis very unlikely.
122024.m: In lupus, antinuclear antibodies can almost always be detected.

122025.q: What does the Latin word “lupus” in the name of the disease mean?
122025.e: The name dates back to the Middle Ages, when skin ulcers were compared to wolf bites. Erythematosus means “reddened”.
122025.m: Lupus is the Latin word for wolf.

122026.q: Roughly how many out of ten people with systemic lupus erythematosus are women?
122026.e: Lupus affects women around nine times more often than men. It usually starts in young adulthood.

122027.q: How do most medicines against lupus work?
a: They damp down the immune system
122027.e: Because the immune system turns against the body itself, it is slowed down with drugs such as hydroxychloroquine, cortisone or other immunosuppressants.
122027.m: In lupus, the immune system is damped down.

122028.q: What is the dangerous organ involvement called in which lupus attacks the kidneys?
122028.e: In lupus nephritis, immune complexes are deposited in the filtering units of the kidneys and inflame them. Without treatment, kidney function can fail.

122029.q: Which environmental factor can trigger skin rashes and flare-ups in lupus?
122029.e: Many people with lupus are sensitive to light. UV light damages skin cells, whose parts then stimulate the misguided immune system.
122029.m: In lupus, consistent sun protection is important.

122030.q: How does lupus caused by medicines usually develop?
a: It fades after the drug is stopped
It gets worse and worse over time
It is passed on to the children
122030.e: Substances such as hydralazine or procainamide can cause lupus symptoms. After the drug is stopped, these usually disappear.
122030.m: Drug-induced lupus usually fades after the drug is stopped.

122031.q: What kind of disease is Hashimoto's thyroiditis?
a: An autoimmune disease of the thyroid
A viral infection of the liver
An iodine deficiency of the adrenal gland
A bacterial infection of the lungs
122031.e: In Hashimoto's thyroiditis, the body's own immune system attacks the thyroid. It becomes chronically inflamed and is gradually destroyed.
122031.m: Hashimoto's is an autoimmune inflammation of the thyroid.

122032.q: Against which thyroid enzyme are the typical antibodies in Hashimoto's thyroiditis directed?
122032.e: Anti-TPO antibodies are directed against thyroid peroxidase, which builds iodine into the thyroid hormones. They are raised in most of those affected.
122032.m: In Hashimoto's, antibodies against thyroid peroxidase are found.

122033.q: Which disorder of function does Hashimoto's thyroiditis usually lead to in the long run?
122033.e: The immune system gradually destroys the thyroid tissue. As a result, too few hormones are made.
122033.m: Hashimoto's usually leads to an underactive thyroid.

122034.q: How is an underactive thyroid caused by Hashimoto's thyroiditis treated?
122034.e: The missing hormone T4 is replaced with a tablet. The treatment usually lasts for life.
122034.m: In Hashimoto's, the missing thyroid hormone is replaced.

122035.q: How does the TSH level in the blood change when Hashimoto's thyroiditis has led to an underactive thyroid?
a: It drops to zero every day
122035.e: The pituitary gland notices the lack of hormone and releases more TSH to drive the thyroid. A raised TSH is therefore an early sign.
122035.m: With an underactive thyroid, TSH is raised.

122036.q: Which cells are found in huge numbers in the thyroid tissue in Hashimoto's thyroiditis?
122036.e: The tissue is densely filled with lymphocytes, some of which form real lymph follicles. That is why the disease is also called chronic lymphocytic thyroiditis.
122036.m: In Hashimoto's, lymphocytes move into the thyroid.

122037.q: Which complaint typically fits an underactive thyroid in Hashimoto's thyroiditis?
122037.e: Without enough thyroid hormone, the metabolism runs more slowly; you feel cold easily, are tired and put on weight. A racing heart and trembling fit an overactive thyroid better.
122037.m: With an underactive thyroid, you feel cold easily.

122038.q: In countries with enough iodine, such as Switzerland, what is the most common cause of an underactive thyroid?
122038.e: Because table salt in Switzerland is iodised, iodine deficiency hardly plays a role any more. The most common cause is then Hashimoto's autoimmune inflammation.
122038.m: Where there is enough iodine, Hashimoto's is the most common cause of an underactive thyroid.

a: The body's own antibodies constantly stimulate the thyroid
A lack of iodine makes the thyroid shrink
A tumour of the pituitary gland makes too much TSH
122039.e: Graves' disease is an autoimmune disease. Antibodies imitate the control hormone TSH and drive the thyroid constantly, so that it becomes overactive.
122039.m: In Graves' disease, antibodies constantly stimulate the thyroid.

122040.q: Which three signs are typical of Graves' disease (known in German as Basedow's disease)?
a: Goitre, bulging eyes and a racing heart
Thirst, needing to pass urine and weight gain
122040.e: In 1840 Carl von Basedow described the enlarged thyroid, the bulging eyes and the fast pulse. Not all patients show all three signs.
122040.m: Goitre, bulging eyes and a racing heart are typical of Graves' disease.

122041.q: Which trace element does the thyroid need to make its hormones?
122041.e: Thyroid hormones such as thyroxine contain iodine atoms. That is why iodine is added to table salt in Switzerland.
122041.m: Without iodine, the thyroid cannot make hormones.

122042.q: What makes the eye involvement in Graves' disease clearly worse?
122042.e: In Graves' disease, tissue and muscles behind the eye swell and push it forward. Smoking makes this inflammation clearly worse.
122042.m: Smoking worsens the eye involvement in Graves' disease.

122043.q: What are medicines called that slow down hormone production by the thyroid in Graves' disease?
122043.e: Antithyroid drugs such as thiamazole block the building of iodine into the thyroid hormones. As a result, hormone production falls.
122043.m: Antithyroid drugs slow down the overactive thyroid.

122044.q: Which treatment for Graves' disease destroys thyroid tissue in a targeted way using a radioactive substance?
122044.e: The thyroid takes up the radioactive iodine-131, which irradiates it from the inside. In this way the overactivity is ended permanently.
122044.m: Radioiodine therapy makes use of the thyroid's uptake of iodine.

122045.q: What is the TSH level like in an overactive thyroid caused by Graves' disease?
a: It is raised but cannot be measured
122045.e: The large amounts of thyroid hormones inhibit the pituitary gland, which therefore releases hardly any TSH. The antibodies still keep driving the thyroid.
122045.m: In Graves' disease, TSH is suppressed.

122046.q: Which complaint typically fits the overactive thyroid in Graves' disease?
122046.e: The metabolism runs at full speed, so those affected lose weight despite a good appetite. Restlessness, sweating and trembling often come on top.
122046.m: With an overactive thyroid, you lose weight despite your appetite.

122047.q: Which defence cells trigger a contact allergy?
122047.e: Contact allergy is driven by T cells, not by antibodies. It therefore belongs to the delayed-type allergies (type IV).
122047.m: In contact allergy, T cells are at work.

122048.q: Which substance is one of the most common causes of contact allergy in Europe?
122048.e: Nickel is found in costume jewellery, belt buckles and buttons. That is why European law limits how much nickel such objects may release.
122048.m: Nickel is a very common cause of contact allergy.

122049.q: Which test is used to detect a contact allergy?
122049.e: In the patch test, test substances are stuck onto the back with plasters. The result is read after about two to three days.
122049.m: Contact allergies are detected with the patch test.

122050.q: How long after contact does it usually take for allergic contact eczema to become visible?
122050.e: T cells first have to move to the spot and release messenger substances. That is why the eczema appears with a delay.
122050.m: Contact eczema only shows after days.

122051.q: What are small molecules called that only become a complete allergen by binding to the body's own proteins?
122051.e: Haptens such as nickel ions are too small on their own to trigger an immune response. Bound to skin proteins, they are recognised by T cells.
122051.m: Haptens only become allergens together with proteins.

122052.q: Which component of cement used to cause “bricklayer's itch” (cement eczema) very often?
122052.e: Hexavalent chromium in cement is a strong contact allergen. Since cement has been made low in chromate, bricklayer's itch has become rarer.
122052.m: Chromate in cement causes bricklayer's itch.

122053.q: Why do experts warn against “black henna” for temporary tattoos?
a: It can cause a strong contact allergy
It colours the skin for ever
It makes the skin sensitive to light as with sunburn
122053.e: The dye p-phenylenediamine (PPD) is often added to black henna. It can cause severe eczema and a lifelong allergy, for example to hair dyes.
122053.m: Black henna can cause a lifelong contact allergy.

122054.q: Apart from preservatives, which group of substances in cosmetics causes contact allergies especially often?
122054.e: Fragrances are among the most common contact allergens. In the patch test, several of them are tested together as a fragrance mix.
122054.m: Fragrances are among the common contact allergens.

122055.q: At which receptor do the classic antihistamines against allergies act?
122055.e: Anti-allergy antihistamines occupy the H1 receptor so that histamine has less effect there. Itching, sneezing and weals ease.
122055.m: Anti-allergy antihistamines act at the H1 receptor.

122056.q: Which side effect is especially common with first-generation antihistamines?
122056.e: Older antihistamines easily reach the brain and reduce alertness there. Newer substances hardly cross the blood-brain barrier.
122056.m: Old antihistamines often make you drowsy.

122057.q: Which substance is a second-generation antihistamine?
122057.e: Cetirizine makes you much less drowsy than older first-generation substances. It is often used for hay fever.
122057.m: Cetirizine is a modern antihistamine that causes little drowsiness.

122058.q: What are H2 antihistamines such as famotidine used for?
122058.e: H2 receptors are found, among other places, on the acid-producing cells of the stomach. If they are blocked, less acid is made.

122059.q: Which Swiss-born pharmacologist received the Nobel Prize in 1957, partly for developing the first antihistamines?
122059.e: Daniel Bovet was born in 1907 in Fleurier in the canton of Neuchâtel. He researched the first antihistamines in Paris and received the Nobel Prize in Medicine in 1957.
122059.m: Daniel Bovet from Neuchâtel was a pioneer of antihistamines.

122060.q: What is the antihistamine dimenhydrinate often taken for?
122060.e: Dimenhydrinate damps down the vomiting centre and the organ of balance. It is therefore taken before car or boat journeys.

122061.q: Which first-generation antihistamine is contained in many over-the-counter sleeping pills because of its sedating effect?
122061.e: Diphenhydramine easily reaches the brain and blocks H1 receptors there, which promote alertness. This side effect is used on purpose in sleeping pills.
122061.m: Diphenhydramine is used as a sleeping aid because it makes you drowsy.

122062.q: In an allergy, which cells release the histamine whose effect antihistamines slow down?
122062.e: Mast cells sit in the skin and mucous membranes and store histamine in granules. When an allergen binds to their IgE antibodies, they release the histamine.
122062.m: Mast cells release histamine in allergies.

122170.q: According to Christian Körner, which factor mainly determines the position of the natural tree line worldwide?
a: The temperature during the growing season
122170.e: Körner showed that the tree line worldwide lies at similarly low temperatures during the growing season. Trees can then no longer build enough new tissue.
122170.m: The tree line is determined mainly by temperature.

122171.q: What was the crane in the forest at Hofstetten near Basel, where Körner's group did research, used for?
a: For adding CO2 to tree crowns
122171.e: With the Swiss Canopy Crane, extra CO2 was released into the crowns of tall trees. This made it possible to test whether a mature forest grows faster with more CO2.
122171.m: The Basel crane was used to study the effect of more CO2 on old trees.

122172.q: How does Christian Körner define the alpine zone in the same way everywhere in the world?
a: As the area above the natural tree line
As the area above 2000 m above sea level
As the area with snow in July
As the area above the snow line
122172.e: Because fixed altitudes do not fit at every latitude, Körner uses the climatic tree line as the lower limit of the alpine zone.
122172.m: The alpine zone begins above the natural tree line.

122173.q: According to Körner, which environmental factor changes with altitude in the same regular way everywhere on Earth, unlike rainfall, for example?
122173.e: Körner distinguished factors that depend directly on altitude, such as air pressure and temperature, from factors linked to altitude only in some regions, such as rainfall or wind.
122173.m: Air pressure falls evenly with altitude everywhere.

122174.q: According to Körner's theory, which process limits plant growth first in the cold?
122174.e: At low temperatures a plant can still make sugar but can hardly turn it into new tissue. Tissue formation, the so-called sink, is the bottleneck.
122174.m: In the cold, plants do not lack sugar but cell growth.

122175.q: Which country does the plant ecologist Christian Körner originally come from?
122175.e: Christian Körner was born in Austria and studied in Innsbruck before moving to Basel.
122175.m: Christian Körner was born in Austria.

122176.q: What does the international programme GLORIA study on mountain summits?
a: How plant life is changing due to climate change
How fast the glaciers are melting
How many climbers visit the summits
How rock is weathered by frost
122176.e: GLORIA is a worldwide network that observes the plant life of mountain summits over the long term to detect the effects of climate change.
122176.m: GLORIA observes the plants on mountain summits around the world.

122177.q: Why are mountain summits especially good places to observe the effects of climate change on plants?
a: Cold-adapted species there react sensitively to warming
Most of Europe's plant species grow there
No rain or snow ever falls on summits
Summit plants grow exactly the same every year
122177.e: On summits, species live at their cold limit. Even small changes in temperature shift which species can grow there. The GLORIA network is coordinated from Vienna.
122177.m: Summit plants show early how climate change is working.

122178.q: Why does GLORIA record the plants on the same plots again and again?
a: To detect changes over the years
Because the plants would otherwise die
To measure the height of the summits again
122178.e: In each region, several summits at different altitudes are studied. The surveys are repeated on the same plots every few years, so changes become visible.

122179.q: On what principle are the summits of a GLORIA region chosen?
a: In steps from the tree line up to the nival zone
All summits at exactly the same altitude
Only the highest summits in each country
Only summits with a cable car
122179.e: The summits range from around the tree line up into the nival zone. In this way a whole altitude gradient is covered.
122179.m: GLORIA summits form a staircase from the tree line to the permanent snow.

122180.q: What are permanently marked plots called, on which researchers record the plants again and again over many years?
122180.e: Permanent monitoring plots are marked precisely and surveyed regularly. In GLORIA they are squares with sides of one metre just below the summits.
122180.m: On permanent plots, the same spot is recorded again and again.

122181.q: What have researchers been observing in the plant life on many Alpine summits for decades?
a: Warmth-loving species from lower altitudes are increasing
Forests are now growing on the summits
122181.e: Warmth-loving species from lower altitudes are increasing, while cold-loving ones are becoming rarer. As a result, the plant community is becoming more warmth-loving.
122181.m: Because of warming, summit communities are becoming more warmth-loving.

122182.q: What did a study of around 300 European summits, published in “Nature” in 2018, show?
a: The number of species is increasing faster and faster
The number of species is falling sharply
The number of species stays the same
122182.e: New species from lower altitudes arrived on the summits studied, and this increase accelerated in step with warming.
122182.m: The number of plant species on Europe's summits is growing faster and faster.

122183.q: According to a GLORIA study from 2012, in which mountains did the number of species on summits decrease?
122183.e: In northern and temperate mountains the number of species increased. In the Mediterranean region it decreased, probably because of growing drought.
122183.m: In the Mediterranean region, summits are losing plant species because of drought.

122184.q: What is meant by frost drought?
a: Drying out when the ground is frozen
Freezing because of ice in the cells
Dying from the weight of snow
122184.e: When the ground is frozen, the roots cannot take up water. If the plant still loses water through its leaves, it dries out.
122184.m: Frost drought means dying of thirst in winter.

122185.q: When does frost drought occur most often at the tree line?
a: In late winter on sunny days
On spring nights when it rains
122185.e: In late winter the sun is already strong, but the ground is still frozen. The water balance then becomes strongly negative.
122185.m: Sunny days in late winter are the most dangerous for frost drought.

122186.q: Why do needles lose a lot of water on sunny winter days?
122186.e: Sunlight can warm needles well above the air temperature. As a result water evaporates, which cannot be replaced from the frozen ground.
122186.m: In winter, the sun's warmth drives the evaporation from needles.

122187.q: Why are young needles at the tree line particularly vulnerable to frost drought?
a: Their wax layer has not fully developed
122187.e: Because of the short summer, the protective cuticle does not develop fully. More water is lost through it in winter.
122187.m: An immature cuticle lets water escape from needles in winter.

122188.q: Why do no trees grow above the tree line, even though dwarf shrubs thrive there?
a: Trees stick out of the protective snow cover and suffer from cold and drying out
The soil there contains no water
There is too much oxygen there
Trees need more sun than there is there
122188.e: Dwarf shrubs stay protected under the snow in winter. Trees stick out and are exposed to cold, wind and frost drought, and the short growing season is no longer enough.
122188.m: At the tree line, trees lack the protection of the snow cover.

122189.q: Which parts of a tree at the tree line are best protected from frost drought?
122189.e: Under the snow it is dark, damp and evenly cool. There the needles hardly lose any water.
122189.m: Under the snow, branches are protected from drying out.

122190.q: How can you recognise damage from frost drought in spring?
a: By white spots on the bark
122190.e: Dried-out needles turn reddish-brown and later fall off. Often only the parts above the snow cover are affected.
122190.m: Frost drought shows up as brown needles.

122191.q: What protects evergreen garden plants such as cherry laurel from frost drought?
122191.e: Evergreen plants lose water through evaporation even in winter. Watering on frost-free days and providing shade make up for the loss.
122191.m: Evergreen plants need water in winter too.

122192.q: What triggers the frost hardening of mountain plants in autumn?
122192.e: The plants react to the shortening days and the first cold. They then gradually build up protective substances and become more frost-hardy.
122192.m: Short days and cold make plants frost-hardy in autumn.

122193.q: In many frost-tolerant plants, where does ice form so that the cells survive?
122193.e: If ice forms between the cells, water is drawn out of the cells without ice crystals destroying them. Ice inside a cell would be deadly.
122193.m: Frost-hardy plants only let ice form between their cells.

122194.q: Why do plants store sugar in their cells in winter?
122194.e: Dissolved sugar lowers the freezing point of the cell sap and stabilises membranes. This lets the cells survive lower temperatures.
122194.m: In plant cells, sugar works like antifreeze.

122195.q: What is it called when water cools below 0 °C without forming ice, which some plant tissues make use of?
122195.e: Pure water in small spaces can stay liquid below 0 °C as long as there are no ice nuclei. Some tissues survive light frost in this way.
122195.m: Supercooled water stays liquid below zero degrees.

122196.q: Which Alpine plant often pushes its flowers through the melting snow cover in spring?
122196.e: The snowbell (Soldanella) starts growing while still under the snow. Its violet bells often appear in small holes in the old snow.
122196.m: The snowbell flowers right through the snow.

122197.q: What advantage do cushion plants such as moss campion have in high mountains?
a: It is warmer and calm inside the cushion
They store salt against the frost
122197.e: The dense, dome-shaped form slows the wind and stores heat. Inside it is much warmer than in the surrounding air.
122197.m: A cushion is a small greenhouse for the plant.

122198.q: What are red pigments such as anthocyanins in the leaves of many high mountain plants for?
122198.e: Anthocyanins work like a sunscreen. They filter high-energy light and so protect the leaf tissue.
122198.m: Red pigments protect mountain plants from strong radiation.

122199.q: Which evergreen dwarf shrub grows on windswept ridges in the Alps that are often free of snow in winter?
122199.e: The trailing azalea, also called alpine azalea, survives extreme cold and wind without protective snow. It is typical of wind-exposed edges.
122199.m: The trailing azalea survives on snow-free windy ridges.

122200.q: On average, by how much does the air temperature in the Alps fall for every 100 m of altitude?
122200.e: Rising air expands and cools. On average the temperature falls by about 0.6 °C for every 100 m.
122200.m: For every 100 metres of altitude it gets about 0.6 degrees colder on average.

122201.q: At an altitude of 400 m the temperature is 14 °C. With a drop of 0.6 °C per 100 m, what temperature would you expect at 2500 m?
122201.e: The difference in altitude is 2100 m, so 21 times 0.6 °C equals 12.6 °C. 14 °C minus 12.6 °C equals 1.4 °C.
122201.m: Multiply the number of hundreds of metres by the drop per 100 m.

122202.q: How does the length of the growing season change with increasing altitude?
122202.e: Higher up, the snow lies longer and autumn starts earlier. So the plants have less time to grow and flower.
122202.m: The higher up, the shorter the plants' growing season.

122203.q: Which vegetation is typical of the subalpine zone of the Swiss Alps?
a: Coniferous forest up to the tree line
122203.e: The subalpine zone is dominated by spruce, larch and Swiss stone pine and reaches up to the tree line.
122203.m: The subalpine zone is the zone of coniferous forest.

122204.q: At an altitude of 5500 m, by roughly how much is air pressure lower than at sea level?
122204.e: Air pressure roughly halves every 5500 m. At this altitude it is only about 500 hPa.
122204.m: At 5500 m, air pressure is about half as high as at sea level.

122205.q: How does UV radiation change with increasing altitude?
122205.e: With altitude, the layer of air above becomes thinner and filters out less UV radiation. Reflection from snow adds to this.
122205.m: The higher you climb, the stronger the UV radiation.

122206.q: Why are altitude gradients in the mountains good natural experiments for climate research?
a: The climate changes a lot over a short distance
The soils are the same everywhere
122206.e: A few hundred metres of altitude correspond to large temperature differences, for which you would have to travel hundreds of kilometres on flat land. This makes it possible to compare climate effects in a small area.
122206.m: A mountainside shows many climate zones over a short distance.

122207.q: Why is it often colder on the valley floor than on the slope above in Alpine valleys in winter?
a: Because of a pool of cold air during an inversion
Because of stronger sunshine down below
Because of warm glacier air above
Because of higher air pressure on the slope
122207.e: Cold, heavy air flows into the valleys at night and collects there. Above it lies warmer air, so for once the temperature rises with altitude.
122207.m: During an inversion, the cold air lies at the bottom of the valley.

122208.q: How does the partial pressure of carbon dioxide in the air change with increasing altitude?
122208.e: The proportion of CO2 in the air stays almost the same, but because the total pressure falls, the partial pressure of CO2 falls too. This makes photosynthesis slightly harder.
122208.m: At altitude, plants have less CO2 pressure available.

122209.q: Which flowering plant was found on the Dom in Valais at about 4500 m and is considered the highest-growing flowering plant in the Alps?
122209.e: Purple saxifrage forms small cushions with violet flowers. It has been recorded on the Dom at about 4500 m.
122209.m: Purple saxifrage flowers higher than any other plant in the Alps.

122210.q: Which plant with white to pink flowers grows in the Alps at over 4000 m, for example on the Finsteraarhorn?
122210.e: Glacier crowfoot is one of the highest-growing flowering plants in Europe and grows on silicate scree.
122210.m: Glacier crowfoot grows at over 4000 m.

122211.q: How was it first proved that summit plants are moving upwards because of warming?
a: By comparison with old species lists
By measuring the thickness of glaciers
